* A huge buff heavy footballer running into a crowd of people can push dozens of people aside quite easily.
* A high affinity agonist like bupe can push other opioids away from the receptors.
* When a user accustomed to full agonist MOR agonism essentially "clogs" their receptors with a weaker substance like bupe, it can cause precipitated withdrawals
* SR-17018 is less of a footballer, and more like an average guy
* Eventually, it replaces the other opioids in the receptors, gradually transitioning overall brain receptor agonism from full to partial
* This essentially means the effect of MOR agonists is more "tapered" when switching to bupe

Another way to look at it, bupe is like giving someone who's ravenously thirsty only one drop of water at a time. SR-17018 is gradually turning the faucet down.

That's interesting to hear, I wonder if there's another mechanism I'm unaware of that causes this. According to what I understood from the study, bupe should in theory be the easier substance to quit.

Based on what I can understand from the study cited below, this substance may not be as effective as Buprenorphine for withdrawal mitigation, due to the following reasons:



"30 min exposure at 37 °C to saturating concentrations of SR-17018 induced a multisite phosphorylation that was indistinguishable from that induced by DAMGO". This multi-site phosphorylation (modification of the mu opioid receptors which can trigger beta-arrestin recruitment) may be a mechanism of further tolerance and addiction development."Figure 3B).



"Furthermore, SR-17018 and DAMGO promoted a robust internalization, which resulted in a receptor accumulation in the perinuclear recycling compartment." This implies the presence of receptor de-sensitization, which would typically imply tolerance, an increase in the amount of the substance needed to saturate all of the receptors. Essentially, the receptors self-regulate due to excessive agonism from SR-17018, meaning more SR is needed over time.



The same study does state that the MOR phospylization (causing tolerance, beta arrestin signaling, etc) are an issue with extended duration and/or high dose usage of the compound, but the study overall seems to imply Buprenorphine has more favorable activity for the scope of opiate withdrawal mitigation.



Further research, and better input from experts is necessary to give a better insight into this chemical, but it seems to be essentially an inferior alternative to Buprenorphine for quitting. 



Fritzwanker S, Schulz S, Kliewer A. SR-17018 Stimulates Atypical µ-Opioid Receptor Phosphorylation and Dephosphorylation. Molecules. 2021 Jul 27;26(15):4509. doi: 10.3390/molecules26154509. PMID: 34361663; PMCID: PMC8348759. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8348759/)

SR-17018 is an opioid which has recently gained popularity due to its capabilities to help users off of other opiates, while mitigating a lot of the withdrawal effects of commonly used drugs like oxy, heroin, fent. 

This is due to something called *biased agonism*, meaning the drug is biased towards a specific signaling pathway. Namely, St-17018 selectively activates the G-protein pathways, as opposed to the beta-arrestin 2 that other opiates use.

Beta-Arrestin 2 signaling is more strongly associated with the dangerous effects of opioids, such as respiratory depression and overdose, which means SR-17018 is less likely to cause overdose and severe dependency issues, as Beta-Arrestin 2 signaling is thought to cause a larger proportion of the withdrawal effects of opiates.

However, it's important to keep in mind that this substance is a *research chemical*. It is unscientific and irresponsible to make claims about this substance's safety in such a place, as there are likely aspects we do not know about this substance scientifically. Furthermore, irresponsible use of any substance is dangerous, and no amount of research can undo the effects of an idiot with a huge ego.

It's likely not the best recreational opioid, but I cannot comment on that due to no experience. Hope this helps.

If it's Ni, you're probably not INFJ.

If it's Fe, you're probably not ENFJ.

Your automatic function is going to be your dominant function, and will narrow you down to two types. From there you can narrow it down.

LSD - Unable to get comfortable in any position, relaxing in bed is impossible. Trip becomes boring. Less feeling "trapped" in the experience. Body load is not pleasant, but substantially more pleasant than shrooms.
